intro: Concise Notes for Competitive Exams — Extended Edition (lectures + online material, diagrams, MCQs & links)
Master handbook covering: Environmental Engineering + Exam Practice Pack
Overlapping topics have been merged into one chapter and repeated points removed. Practice MCQs for all parts are near the end; the answer key is the last chapter.

b: Domestic (largest share, ~50–60% of total), industrial, commercial & institutional, public use, fire demand, losses & wastage (~15–20%)
Per capita demand (lpcd) = total annual water required ÷ (365 × population)
Factors affecting per capita demand: city size, climate, living standard, industries, metering, pressure, cost, sewerage system
Maximum daily demand = 1.8 × average daily demand
Maximum hourly demand = 1.5 × max daily = 2.7 × average daily
Goodrich formula: p = 180 t^(−0.10) (p = % of annual average, t = days, 1/24 to 365)
Source & intake designed for max daily; distribution system for max hourly (or max daily + fire)

s.t: Fire Demand (Q in L/min, P = population in thousands)
b: National Board of Fire Underwriters: Q = 4637 √P (1 − 0.01 √P)
Dams/large storage: 50 years | Pipelines & distribution: 30 years | Treatment units: 15 years | Pumps: 15 years
Arithmetic increase: Pn = P0 + n·x̄ — old, large, saturated cities (gives low values)
Geometric increase: Pn = P0 (1 + r/100)^n — young, rapidly growing cities (gives high values)
Incremental increase: Pn = P0 + n·x̄ + [n(n+1)/2]·ȳ — average cities (most realistic of the three)
Others: decreasing rate of growth, simple graphical, comparative graphical, ratio/correlation, master plan/zoning, logistic (S-curve)
Logistic saturation population: Ps = [2P0P1P2 − P1²(P0 + P2)] ÷ (P0P2 − P1²)
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

Typical per-capita demand: ≈ 135 L/person/day is a common design value for towns with full flushing; ≈ 40–70 lpcd for stand-post/rural supplies; large cities 150–200+ lpcd. Pakistan WASAs often design with ≈ 150–250 L/c/d (incl. losses).
Breakdown of domestic use: Drinking ≈ 5 L, cooking ≈ 5 L, bathing ≈ 55 L, washing clothes ≈ 20 L, utensils ≈ 10 L, house washing ≈ 10 L, flushing ≈ 30 L (≈ 135 L total).
Non-revenue water (NRW): Leakage + theft + metering errors; often 30–50% in South-Asian cities — leak detection and metering reduce it.
Geometric: Growth rates ≈ 30%, 26.9%, 24.2% per decade → r̄ ≈ 27% → P ≈ 82,000 × 1.27 ≈ 1,04,000 (gives the highest value).
Geometric method gives the HIGHEST forecast (young, growing cities); arithmetic the LOWEST (old, saturated cities); incremental lies between.
Surface: rivers, streams, lakes, impounding reservoirs
Sub-surface: springs, infiltration galleries, infiltration wells, wells (shallow, deep, tube, artesian)
Aquiclude: stores but does not transmit (clay)
Aquitard: stores, transmits very slowly (sandy clay)
Darcy's law: V = K·i ; Q = K·i·A
Dupuit – unconfined aquifer: Q = πK(H² − h²) ÷ ln(R/r)
Dupuit – confined aquifer: Q = 2πKb(H − h) ÷ ln(R/r)
Transmissivity T = K × b ; Storage coefficient S (confined: very small, 10⁻⁵–10⁻³)
Darcy-Weisbach: hf = f L V² ÷ (2 g D)
Cast/ductile iron: most common for mains; GI for house connections; PVC/HDPE for small sizes; RCC/steel for large mains
Water hammer: sudden pressure rise on rapid valve closure; controlled by surge tanks, relief valves, slow closing valves
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Intakes: River intake, reservoir intake (tower), lake intake, canal intake; located upstream of town outfalls, with screens and bell-mouth entry.
Pumps: Centrifugal (most common in water works), reciprocating (high head, small discharge), submersible (tube wells), jet, air-lift.
Economical diameter of rising main: Lea’s formula D = (0.97–1.22)√Q (D in m, Q in m³/s).
Pipe joints: Socket-and-spigot (CI), flanged (pumps), expansion, flexible, mechanical (Dresser) joints.
Corrosion of pipes: Tuberculation in CI/steel; prevented by lining (cement mortar, bitumen), cathodic protection, pH control.
Hazen-Williams C: new CI ≈ 130, old CI ≈ 100, PVC/HDPE ≈ 140–150. Water hammer pressure rise is controlled by surge tanks, slow valve closure and air vessels.
Turbidity: NTU; measured by Jackson candle turbidimeter, nephelometer (most accurate)
Colour: platinum-cobalt scale (TCU); taste & odour: threshold odour number (TON)
TDS: affects palatability; measured by evaporation or conductivity (TDS ≈ 0.55–0.7 × EC µS/cm)
Hardness (mg/L as CaCO3): due to Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺
Temporary (carbonate): bicarbonates of Ca, Mg — removed by boiling
Permanent (non-carbonate): sulphates, chlorides, nitrates of Ca, Mg
Soft 0–75 | Moderately hard 75–150 | Hard 150–300 | Very hard > 300
Fluoride: < 1 mg/L → dental caries; > 1.5 mg/L → fluorosis
Nitrate: > 45 mg/L (as NO3) → methaemoglobinaemia (blue baby syndrome)
Iron (0.3) & manganese (0.1 mg/L): staining of clothes and fixtures, taste
Arsenic: skin lesions, cancer (major groundwater issue in Punjab/Sindh)
Coliform bacteria (E. coli) = indicator of faecal contamination
MPN test (multiple tube fermentation): presumptive → confirmed → completed
Membrane filter technique: direct colony count
Waterborne diseases: cholera, typhoid, dysentery, hepatitis A & E, polio, giardiasis
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Alkalinity: Due to OH⁻, CO₃²⁻, HCO₃⁻; phenolphthalein (P) & methyl orange (total, T) titration — P = 0 → only bicarbonate.
Chlorides: Mohr’s method (silver nitrate, potassium chromate indicator); sudden rise indicates sewage pollution.
Indicator organism: E. coli / faecal coliforms; drinking water should have 0 per 100 mL.
Arsenic in Pakistan: Groundwater in parts of Punjab and Sindh exceeds safe limits; WHO guideline 10 µg/L (Pakistan NSDWQ allows 50 µg/L).
Methaemoglobinaemia (blue-baby) — nitrates; fluorosis — fluoride > 1.5 mg/L; Minamata — mercury; Itai-itai — cadmium; arsenicosis — arsenic.
Intake & screening → aeration → coagulation (flash mix) → flocculation → sedimentation → filtration → disinfection → storage & distribution
Removes CO2, H2S, taste & odour; oxidises Fe and Mn
Types: spray aerators, cascade/multiple tray, diffused air
Stokes' law (d < 0.1 mm): Vs = g (Gs − 1) d² ÷ (18 ν)
Surface overflow rate = Q/A; ideal tank efficiency depends on overflow rate, not depth
Detention time = V/Q: plain sedimentation 4–8 h; with coagulation 2–4 h
Overflow rate: plain 12–18 m³/m²/day; with coagulation 24–40 m³/m²/day
Settling types: Type I discrete, Type II flocculent, Type III zone (hindered), Type IV compression
Alum Al2(SO4)3·18H2O — most common; effective pH 6.5–8.5
Ferrous sulphate (copperas): pH > 8.5; ferric chloride / ferric sulphate: wide pH range
Coagulant aids: polyelectrolytes, activated silica, bentonite clay
Optimum dose found by jar test
Mechanisms: charge neutralisation, sweep floc, bridging
Velocity gradient G = √(P ÷ μV); flocculator G = 20–80 s⁻¹, Gt = 10⁴–10⁵
Pressure filter: closed steel vessel; small plants, industries, swimming pools
Dual/multimedia: anthracite over sand — longer filter runs
Operational troubles: mud balls, air binding (negative head), cracking of sand bed
Chlorine: Cl2 + H2O → HOCl + HCl ; HOCl ⇌ H⁺ + OCl⁻
HOCl is ~80 times more effective than OCl⁻; low pH (< 7.5) favours HOCl
Chlorine demand = chlorine applied − residual chlorine
Free residual chlorine: 0.2–0.5 mg/L at consumer end; contact time ≥ 30 min
Break-point chlorination: chlorine added beyond point where all ammonia/organics are oxidised; residual is free chlorine
Super-chlorination: excess dose during epidemics, followed by dechlorination (SO2, sodium thiosulphate, sodium bisulphite, activated carbon)
Chlorine forms: liquid/gas chlorine, bleaching powder CaOCl2 (~30–35% available Cl), sodium hypochlorite, chloramines, chlorine dioxide
Other disinfectants: ozone (strongest, no residual), UV rays, boiling, silver (Katadyn process), iodine/bromine (small supplies)
Softening: lime-soda process (lime → carbonate hardness; soda ash → non-carbonate); zeolite/base exchange (zero hardness, regenerated by NaCl brine); ion exchange demineralisation
Fe & Mn removal: aeration + sedimentation + filtration
Defluoridation: Nalgonda technique (alum + lime), activated alumina; fluoridation ~1 mg/L
Taste & odour: activated carbon, aeration, KMnO4; algae control: copper sulphate
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 4.1 — Sequence of units in a conventional water treatment plant with typical design values.
Rapid sand filter design: Rate ≈ 5–7.5 m³/m²/h (≈ 3000–4800 L/m²/h); effective size 0.45–0.7 mm; uniformity coefficient 1.3–1.7; backwash when head loss ≈ 2.5–3 m.
Slow sand filter: Rate ≈ 2.4–4.8 m³/m²/day (≈ 100–200 L/m²/h); schmutzdecke (biological layer) does the work; scraped, not backwashed.
Alum dose: ≈ 10–30 mg/L typical; produces floc Al(OH)₃ and consumes alkalinity.
Zeolite (base exchange): Removes both temporary & permanent hardness to zero hardness; regenerated with brine (NaCl).
Rapid sand filter is ≈ 30–40 times faster than slow sand filter but needs coagulation; bacterial removal: slow sand 98–99%, rapid 80–90%.
Dead-end / tree system: old towns; simple, cheap; stagnation at dead ends
Grid-iron system: no dead ends, water circulates; more valves & pipes; best for planned towns
Ring / circular system: well-planned towns; any point fed from two directions
Radial system: area divided into zones, each fed from a central reservoir — high pressure, quick service
Gravity, pumping without storage, combined pumping & storage (most common)
Continuous supply preferred; intermittent supply causes contamination risk
Hardy Cross method: pipe networks (loops) — balancing head loss / flow corrections
Equivalent pipe method: replace series/parallel pipes by single pipe
Balancing/service reservoir capacity: mass curve method
Check/reflux (non-return) valve: one-way flow, on pump delivery
Air relief valve: at summits; scour/drain valve: at low points
Pressure relief valve: protects against high pressure; butterfly valve: large pipes
Residual pressure at ferrule: 7 m (1 storey), 12 m (2 storeys), 17 m (3 storeys)
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 5.1 — Distribution layouts: dead-end, grid-iron, ring and radial systems.
Storage: Service reservoir capacity = balancing storage (from mass curve) + breakdown storage + fire storage.
Overhead tanks: Elevated tanks (Intze tank for large capacity) provide pressure and balancing.
Leak detection: Sounding rods, aqua-phones, district metered areas (DMA), pressure management.
Hardy Cross: head-loss correction Δ = −Σ(kQⁿ)/(nΣkQⁿ⁻¹) applied loop by loop until losses balance.
Sewage: liquid waste including human excreta; sullage: kitchen & bath water without excreta
Sewer: pipe carrying sewage; sewerage: entire system of collection, treatment, disposal
Systems: separate (sanitary & storm separate), combined, partially separate
Dry weather flow (DWF) = 75–80% of water supplied
Babbitt peak factor: M = 5 ÷ P^0.2 (P in thousands)
Harmon peak factor: PF = 1 + 14 ÷ (4 + √P) (P in thousands)
Storm water – Rational method: Q = C I A ÷ 360 (Q m³/s, I mm/h, A hectares)
Time of concentration = inlet time + time of flow in drain
Runoff coefficient C: roofs 0.7–0.95, paved roads 0.8–0.9, lawns/parks 0.05–0.35
Manning: V = (1/n) R^(2/3) S^(1/2) — most used for sewers
Non-scouring (maximum) velocity: ~2.5–3 m/s (depends on pipe material)
Sanitary sewers designed running 1/2 to 3/4 full (never full)
Circular section most common; egg-shaped: combined sewers (better velocity at low flow)
Vitrified clay (stoneware): house sewers, smooth, corrosion resistant, weak in tension
RCC/concrete: large sewers; suffer crown corrosion (H2S → H2SO4)
Cast iron/ductile iron: under heavy loads, pressure mains, crossings
Manholes: at junctions, changes in direction/gradient/size; spacing ~30 m (small) up to 300 m (very large)
Drop manhole: when incoming sewer is > 0.6 m above outgoing
Lamp holes, clean-outs, street inlets/gully pits, catch basins, flushing tanks, grease & oil traps
Inverted siphon (depressed sewer): crossing rivers/valleys; velocity ≥ ~1 m/s
Testing of sewers: water test, smoke test, air test, ball test
Traps (water seal 25–75 mm): P, Q, S, nahani (floor), gully, intercepting trap
Plumbing systems: one-pipe, two-pipe, single-stack, partially ventilated one-pipe
Vent pipe: prevents loss of seal by siphonage/back pressure
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Minimum cover over sewers: ≈ 0.9–1.0 m under roads (protection from traffic loads and frost).
Manhole spacing: ≈ 30 m for small sewers (≤ 0.9 m dia) up to ≈ 90–300 m for large sewers.
Crown corrosion: H₂S → oxidised to H₂SO₄ on crown of concrete sewers; prevented by ventilation, adequate velocity, PVC/vitrified pipes, coatings.
Storm sewers: Designed running full; flushing tanks and self-cleansing velocity prevent deposition in sanitary sewers.
Self-cleansing velocity ≈ 0.6–0.9 m/s; maximum velocity ≈ 2.5–3 m/s. Sanitary sewers never designed to run full — ½ to ¾ full at peak.
Fresh sewage: grey, musty odour; stale/septic: dark/black, H2S smell
Nitrogen forms: organic & ammonia (fresh) → nitrite (being oxidised) → nitrate (well oxidised, stable)
Oxygen required by microbes to stabilise biodegradable organic matter (aerobic)
BODt = L0 (1 − 10^(−kt)), k ≈ 0.1/day (base 10) or 0.23/day (base e) at 20 °C
Temperature correction: kT = k20 × θ^(T − 20), θ = 1.047
BOD = (DOinitial − DOfinal) ÷ P, P = dilution fraction
Population equivalent = industrial BOD (kg/day) ÷ per capita BOD (~0.08 kg/person/day)
COD: chemical oxidation by potassium dichromate in acid; result in ~3 h; COD > BOD
BOD/COD > 0.5 → readily biodegradable; ThOD > COD > BODu > BOD5
DO saturation ≈ 9.1 mg/L at 20 °C; fish need ≥ 4–5 mg/L
Disposal by dilution (rivers, sea) or on land (sewage farming/irrigation)
Self-purification zones: degradation → active decomposition → recovery → clear water
Streeter-Phelps equation: oxygen sag curve; critical point = minimum DO
Factors: dilution, temperature, sunlight, current/turbulence, sedimentation, oxidation
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 7.1 — BOD curve: first-stage carbonaceous BOD and nitrification; BOD₅ ≈ 68% of ultimate (k = 0.1/day, base 10).
Fig. 7.2 — Oxygen sag curve and zones of self-purification downstream of a sewage outfall.
Worked BOD: Sample diluted 2% (P = 0.02); DO₀ = 8.5, DO₅ = 4.5 → BOD₅ = (8.5 − 4.5)/0.02 = 200 mg/L.
Ultimate BOD from BOD₅: L₀ = BOD₅ / (1 − 10^(−5k)); for k = 0.1 → L₀ = BOD₅/0.684.

Dilution method criteria: Dilution factor ratio — no treatment needed if river:sewage flow > 500; primary (plain sedimentation) if 300–500; sedimentation + chemical precipitation if 150–300; complete treatment if < 150 (classic Indian/US guidance).
COD > BOD always (dichromate oxidises non-biodegradable organics). Fresh sewage is slightly alkaline, grey; septic sewage is black, smells of H₂S.
Grit chamber: removes sand/grit (Gs ~2.65); horizontal velocity ~0.3 m/s kept constant by proportional flow weir or Parshall flume; detention 30–60 s
Skimming tank: oil & grease; detention ~3–5 min
Activated Sludge Process (suspended growth): aeration tank + secondary clarifier + return activated sludge
Conventional: MLSS 1500–3000 mg/L; F/M 0.2–0.4; HRT 4–8 h; SRT (mean cell residence time) 5–15 days
SVI 50–150 mL/g = good settling; > 200 = sludge bulking (filamentous organisms)
Variants: complete mix, step aeration, tapered aeration, contact stabilisation, extended aeration (HRT 18–36 h, low F/M), oxidation ditch, SBR, MBBR
Trickling Filter (attached growth): biological oxidation, not true filtration
Rotating Biological Contactor (RBC): rotating discs with biofilm
Waste Stabilisation Ponds: algae–bacteria symbiosis; anaerobic, facultative (1–2 m deep), maturation ponds; ideal for hot climates; low cost, large land
Aerated lagoons; UASB (upflow anaerobic sludge blanket) reactors
Nitrogen removal: nitrification (aerobic) + denitrification (anoxic); ammonia stripping
Phosphorus removal: chemical precipitation (alum, lime, ferric) or biological
Filtration, activated carbon adsorption, membranes, final disinfection
Thickening (gravity, flotation) → digestion → conditioning → dewatering → disposal
Anaerobic digestion stages: hydrolysis → acidogenesis → acetogenesis → methanogenesis
Dewatering: sludge drying beds, vacuum filter, belt press, centrifuge
Volume vs moisture: V1/V2 = (100 − p2) ÷ (100 − p1)
Septic tank: sedimentation + anaerobic digestion; detention ~24 h; desludging every 1–3 years; effluent to soak pit/drain field
Others: cesspool, pit latrine, soak pit
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 8.1 — Units of a sewage treatment plant and the sludge line.
Fig. 8.2 — Activated sludge process: aeration tank, secondary clarifier, return and waste sludge.
Fig. 8.3 — Two-compartment septic tank: scum, clear zone, sludge, baffle, T-pipe inlet and outlet.
Sludge age (SRT): θc = mass of MLSS in system ÷ mass wasted per day; conventional ASP ≈ 5–15 days; extended aeration ≈ 20–30 days.
Sludge volume index: SVI = (settled volume in 30 min, mL/L × 1000) ÷ MLSS (mg/L).
Waste stabilisation ponds (Pakistan): Widely used for small and medium towns in Pakistan — cheap, low energy, but need large land area.
Oxidation ditch: Extended-aeration ASP in a looped channel with rotors; small towns.
Trickling filter = attached growth; ASP = suspended growth; RBC = attached growth on rotating discs; UASB = anaerobic sludge blanket.
Municipal (MSW), industrial, hazardous, biomedical, e-waste, construction & demolition
Garbage: putrescible food waste; rubbish: non-putrescible (combustible paper/plastic, non-combustible glass/metal); ashes
Generation → on-site handling & storage → collection → transfer & transport → processing → disposal
Collection is the costliest element (~70–80% of total cost)
Sanitary landfill: most common; waste spread, compacted, daily cover ~15 cm soil; liner + leachate collection + gas (CH4) venting
Composting: aerobic (Indore, windrow, Bangalore is anaerobic); optimum C/N ratio 25–30; vermicomposting uses earthworms
Incineration: 800–1000 °C; volume reduction 80–90%; energy recovery; air pollution concern
Pyrolysis: thermal decomposition in absence of oxygen
Waste hierarchy: reduce → reuse → recycle → recover → dispose
Biomedical waste: colour-coded segregation; incineration, autoclaving
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 9.1 — Sanitary landfill: liner, leachate collection, compacted waste cells, daily cover, final cap, gas vents.
Composition (South Asia): High organic/food fraction (≈ 50–60%), moisture high, calorific value low — composting more suitable than incineration.
C/N ratio for composting: Optimum ≈ 25–30 : 1; moisture ≈ 50–60%; temperature reaches 55–65 °C (kills pathogens).
Leachate: Liquid percolating through waste — very high BOD/COD; collected & treated.
Pakistan: Waste management companies (e.g., Lahore Waste Management Company, WSSP Peshawar, SWMB Karachi) handle collection; Lakhodair landfill (Lahore) is a well-known engineered site.
Collection & transportation ≈ 70–80% of SWM cost; sanitary landfill is the final, unavoidable disposal step.
Layers: troposphere (0–~12 km, weather) → stratosphere (ozone layer) → mesosphere → thermosphere
Primary: emitted directly — CO, SO2, NOx, hydrocarbons, particulates
Secondary: formed in atmosphere — O3, PAN, smog, H2SO4/HNO3 aerosols
Criteria pollutants (US EPA, 6): CO, Pb, NO2, O3, PM (PM10, PM2.5), SO2
CO: forms carboxyhaemoglobin; affinity for Hb ~210–250 times that of O2
SO2: respiratory irritation, acid rain; NOx: photochemical smog, acid rain
PAN: eye irritation, plant damage; lead: neurological damage
PM2.5: penetrates deep into lungs; most harmful particulate fraction
London (classical) smog: smoke + SO2, cold humid winter, reducing
Photochemical (Los Angeles) smog: NOx + HC + sunlight → O3, PAN; oxidising
Acid rain: pH < 5.6 (normal rain ~5.6 due to CO2)
Greenhouse gases: CO2, CH4, N2O, CFCs, water vapour, O3
Ozone depletion: CFCs (chlorine radicals); ozone measured in Dobson units
Dry adiabatic lapse rate: 9.8 °C/km (~1 °C per 100 m)
Super-adiabatic: unstable; sub-adiabatic: stable; inversion (temperature increases with height): very stable, traps pollutants
Inversion below, unstable above stack — best for dispersion
Inversion above, unstable below stack — worst (pollutants brought to ground)
Inversion both above and below stack
Effective stack height H = h + Δh (plume rise); dispersion by Gaussian plume model
Gaseous control: absorption, adsorption (activated carbon), combustion/incineration
SO2: flue gas desulphurisation (limestone scrubbing); vehicles: catalytic converter (CO, HC, NOx)
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Smog episodes in Pakistan: Winter smog in Lahore and other Punjab cities (Nov–Jan) from vehicle exhaust, industry, brick kilns and crop-residue burning combined with inversions.
Particle collectors: Settling chamber (> 50 µm), cyclone (5–20 µm+), fabric (bag) filter (> 0.1 µm, ≈ 99%), electrostatic precipitator (0.1–1 µm, ≈ 99%), wet scrubber (gases + particles).
Vehicles: Catalytic converter: CO → CO₂, HC → CO₂ + H₂O, NOx → N₂ (three-way).
AQI: Air Quality Index combines PM2.5, PM10, O₃, NO₂, SO₂, CO concentrations into one number.
Fanning plume — strong inversion (stable); looping — super-adiabatic (unstable); coning — neutral/slightly stable; lofting — inversion below stack (best); fumigation — inversion above stack (worst).
Sound level: L = 10 log(I/I0) = 20 log(P/P0); reference pressure P0 = 20 µPa
Audible range: 20 Hz – 20 kHz; threshold of hearing 0 dB; threshold of pain ~120–140 dB
Two equal sources combined: +3 dB; doubling distance (point source): −6 dB
Measured with sound level meter in dB(A); Leq = equivalent continuous level
WHO residential guideline: ~55 dB(A) day, ~45 dB(A) night
Control: at source (silencers, maintenance), along path (barriers, green belts), at receiver (ear plugs/muffs)
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Adding sound levels: L = 10 log Σ10^(Li/10). Example: 80 dB + 80 dB = 83 dB; 80 + 70 dB ≈ 80.4 dB.
Exposure limits: ≈ 85–90 dB(A) for 8 h occupational exposure; every +3 to +5 dB halves the allowed time.
Doubling distance from a point source → −6 dB; from a line source (road) → −3 dB.
Steps: screening → scoping → baseline study → impact prediction → mitigation & EMP → public participation → review → decision → monitoring
IEE (Initial Environmental Examination) for smaller projects; full EIA for major projects
EMP: Environmental Management Plan; ISO 14001: Environmental Management System
Pakistan Environmental Protection Act (PEPA) 1997; Pak-EPA & Pakistan Environmental Protection Council
After 18th Amendment (2010): environment devolved to provinces (provincial EPAs)
NEQS effluent to inland waters (key values): BOD5 80 mg/L, COD 150 mg/L, TSS 200 mg/L, TDS 3500 mg/L, oil & grease 10 mg/L, pH 6–9
Stockholm Conference 1972 — World Environment Day (5 June); UNEP (HQ Nairobi)
Kyoto Protocol 1997 — greenhouse gas reduction targets
Paris Agreement 2015 — limit warming well below 2 °C (aim 1.5 °C)
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

KP & Punjab: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Environmental Protection Act 2014 and Punjab Environmental Protection (Amendment) Act 2012 (post-18th Amendment provincial laws); EPA approval (IEE/EIA) is required before construction.
Schedules (Pakistan IEE/EIA Regulations): Schedule I — projects requiring IEE; Schedule II — projects requiring full EIA (e.g., dams, large highways, power plants).
Climate: Pakistan’s National Climate Change Policy; Ministry of Climate Change & Environmental Coordination; COP-27 (2022) loss-and-damage fund after the 2022 floods.

chapters.t: Plumbing, Rural Sanitation & Water in Buildings
b: Traps & seal: P, Q, S, gully, nahani (floor), intercepting traps; water seal 25–75 mm (≈ 50 mm common).
Loss of trap seal: Self-siphonage, induced siphonage, back pressure, evaporation, capillarity, wind effect — prevented by anti-siphonage/vent pipes.
Rural sanitation: Pit latrine, VIP (ventilated improved pit) latrine, pour-flush latrine, twin-pit latrine, septic tank with soak pit.
Soak pit: Effluent percolation pit filled with brickbats/stone; ≥ 15–20 m away from wells.
Rain-water harvesting: Roof-top collection → first-flush diverter → filter → storage/recharge wells; mandatory for large buildings in some Pakistani cities.
Distance between a water well and a soak pit / septic tank should be ≥ 15 m (more in sandy soils).
Sewage includes excreta; sullage = kitchen/bath waste water only
Sewer = the pipe; sewerage = the whole system
BOD biological (5 d, 20 °C); COD chemical (dichromate, ≈ 3 h); COD > BOD
Biological, no coagulation, scraped vs physical, coagulation, backwashed
Stagnation, cheap vs no dead ends, more valves, reliable
Single storey (settle + digest together) vs two storeys (separate)
Attached growth vs suspended growth with sludge return
Smoke + SO₂, reducing, winter vs NOx + HC + sunlight, oxidising
Inversion at stack (stable) vs inversion above stack trapping smoke at ground (worst)
Max daily 1.8 × avg; max hourly 2.7 × avg; Goodrich p = 180t^−0.10
Arithmetic P₀ + nx̄; geometric P₀(1 + r)ⁿ; incremental P₀ + nx̄ + n(n + 1)ȳ/2
Q = KiA; unconfined Q = πK(H² − h²)/ln(R/r); confined 2πKb(H − h)/ln(R/r)
Vs = g(Gs − 1)d²/(18ν); SOR = Q/A; DT = V/Q
Demand = applied − residual; residual 0.2–0.5 mg/L; kg/d = mg/L × MLD
F/M = QS₀/(VX); HRT = V/Q; SVI = SV(mL/L) × 1000/MLSS(mg/L)

Q = 10 MLD, surface overflow rate 30 m³/m²/day, depth 3 m: A = 10,000/30 = 333 m² (circular D = 20.6 m); volume = 1,000 m³; detention = 1,000/10,000 × 24 = 2.4 h.
Q = 10 MLD = 416.7 m³/h at 5 m³/m²/h → filter area = 83.3 m² (e.g., 4 beds of ≈ 21 m² + one standby).
10 MLD, chlorine demand 0.5 mg/L, residual 0.2 mg/L → dose 0.7 mg/L → 0.7 × 10 = 7 kg/day of chlorine = 7/0.30 ≈ 23.3 kg/day of bleaching powder (30% available chlorine).
Ca²⁺ = 60 mg/L, Mg²⁺ = 18 mg/L → hardness = 60 × 2.5 + 18 × 4.17 = 150 + 75 = 225 mg/L as CaCO₃ (hard water).
Industry discharges 600 kg BOD/day → PE = 600/0.08 = 7,500 persons.

Q = 10,000 m³/d, S₀ = 200 mg/L, F/M = 0.3/d, MLSS = 2,500 mg/L: V = QS₀/(F/M × X) = 10,000 × 200/(0.3 × 2500) = 2,667 m³; HRT = 6.4 h. If settled volume after 30 min = 250 mL/L → SVI = 250 × 1000/2500 = 100 mL/g (good settling).
Thickening sludge from 98% to 95% moisture: V₂/V₁ = (100 − 98)/(100 − 95) = 0.4 → volume falls by 60%.
